title: About this model: the woman
summary: One woman's body, rebuilt in 3D from photographs of thin slices of it.

layers.basics: This woman gave her body to science. After her death it was frozen and cut into thousands of very thin slices, and each slice was photographed. Anatomists later traced her organs slice by slice to make the 3D shapes you see here.
layers.deeper: She is the Visible Human Female of the U.S. National Library of Medicine, released in 1995. The 3D models are the Human Reference Atlas's reference organs for a female body, made from her sections. Some parts were not made from her: her skull, ribs, shoulder, arm, hand and foot bones, almost all her muscles and her stomach are missing, and nothing has been borrowed from anyone else to fill the gaps.
layers.expert: Her brain in the atlas is not her own: it is the Allen Institute's reference brain of another woman, mirrored and resized to fit her head. The inside of each breast is a sculpted reference model placed in her body. The large intestine and the discs between her vertebrae were modelled to fit her, and the atlas makers adjusted her skin to fit her organs. She is shown at the size of the model, 1.66 m from sole to crown; her recorded height was 171.2 cm.

did_you_know: Her slices are a third of a millimetre apart, three times closer than the Visible Human Male's 1 mm, so that each picture element is a small cube.

ext.title: U.S. National Library of Medicine: the Visible Human Project
Human Reference Atlas: 3D reference organs, female (v1.10)

open_questions: One body is one person: how her organs compare with other women's of her age needs many bodies, not one.

title: About this model: the man
summary: One man's body, rebuilt in 3D from his medical scans and scaled to 1.75 m.

layers.basics: The man's shapes come from BodyParts3D, a free anatomy model built from scans of one adult man. It has his skeleton, many muscles and organs, and the vessels of his whole body.
layers.deeper: BodyParts3D was made in Japan from TARO, a set of MRI scans of one adult man. Here it is scaled so that he stands 1.75 m tall. The woman beside him is not scaled, so the two are not drawn to one rule.
layers.expert: Because each model is one person, the differences you see between them are differences between these two people: their age, build, the way each was imaged, and what each atlas chose to model. They are not the average differences between men and women.

facts: BodyParts3D (from the TARO MRI scans of one man)

title: Breast
summary: Fat and gland tissue on the chest wall, with the mammary gland that can make milk.

layers.basics: A breast is mostly fat wrapped round a gland. The gland is a set of lobes whose ducts open on the nipple. How large a breast is depends mostly on its fat, and size has no effect on how much milk it can make.
layers.deeper: The mammary gland is a modified sweat gland. Its lobes hold clusters of milk-making cells (alveoli); ducts from the lobes widen into sinuses and then open on the nipple. Bands of connective tissue run from the gland to the skin and help hold its shape.
layers.expert: Milk is made in the alveoli and carried by 15 to 20 lactiferous ducts to the surface of the nipple. The areola around the nipple carries small glands that secrete a lubricating fluid during breastfeeding. In this model the inside of the breast is a sculpted reference model drawn from anatomy atlases and placed in her body, not traced from her sections.

did_you_know: Breast size is set by fat, not gland: it says nothing about how much milk a breast can make.

title: Mammary lobes
summary: The milk-making parts of the breast's gland.

layers.basics: Each breast holds a set of lobes, the parts of the gland that can make milk. Fat fills the space round them.
layers.deeper: Inside each lobe are clusters of secretory cells called alveoli. Their size changes with how much milk they hold.
layers.expert: The lobes are where milk is made during lactation; outside pregnancy and breastfeeding the gland is small and much of the breast is fat. Here the lobes are part of a sculpted reference model placed in her body.

facts: alveoli, in clusters within each lobe

title: Lactiferous ducts
summary: The tubes that carry milk from the lobes to the nipple.

layers.basics: Milk leaves the gland through a set of small tubes that end on the nipple.
layers.deeper: Each lactiferous duct widens just before the nipple into a lactiferous sinus, where milk collects before it leaves.
layers.expert: Between 15 and 20 of these ducts open on the surface of the nipple. In this model they are part of a sculpted reference model of the breast's inside.

title: Nipple and areola
summary: The raised nipple, where the milk ducts open, and the darker skin round it.

layers.basics: The nipple is where milk comes out. The ring of darker skin round it is the areola.
layers.deeper: The areola is pigmented and usually round. Small glands in it secrete a fluid that keeps the skin supple while a baby feeds.
layers.expert: An areola measures from 25 to 100 mm across. The lactiferous ducts, 15 to 20 of them, open on the nipple's surface.

title: Suspensory ligaments of the breast
summary: Bands of connective tissue that tie the breast's tissue to the skin over it.

layers.basics: Thin bands of tough tissue run through each breast and attach it to the skin, helping to hold its shape.
layers.deeper: They are connective tissue, made mostly of collagen, running from the gland and the tissue round it to the dermis of the skin.
layers.expert: They are named after the surgeon Astley Cooper, who described them. In this model they are part of the sculpted reference model of the breast.

title: Cervix
summary: The narrow lower end of the uterus, which opens into the vagina.

layers.basics: The cervix is the neck of the uterus. It is narrow, and its lower end sticks into the top of the vagina.
layers.deeper: A channel runs through it, from an inner opening into the uterus to an outer opening into the vagina. Its glands make mucus that changes through the menstrual cycle.
layers.expert: When estrogen is high, near ovulation, cervical mucus becomes thin and stringy, which can help sperm move through. In this model it comes from her sections, with its inner and outer openings.

title: Uterine tubes
summary: The two tubes that carry an egg from beside each ovary to the uterus.

layers.basics: Each tube runs from the top of the uterus out to an ovary. Its open end has finger-like fringes that sweep the released egg in. Fertilization often happens inside the tube.
layers.deeper: A tube has three parts: the narrow isthmus next to the uterus, the wider ampulla in the middle, where fertilization often occurs, and the funnel-shaped infundibulum with its fringes (fimbriae) next to the ovary.
layers.expert: Cilia on the tube's lining beat toward the uterus, more strongly around ovulation, and the smooth muscle of its wall contracts every 4 to 8 seconds, moving the egg along. The tube is not attached to the ovary: an egg is released into the space between them.

did_you_know: The open end of each tube is not joined to its ovary; the fringes sweep the egg in.

title: Vagina
summary: The muscular canal from the cervix to the outside of the body.

layers.basics: The vagina is a stretchy muscular tube about 10 cm long that leads from the cervix to the outside.
layers.deeper: Its wall has three layers: a fibrous outer coat, smooth muscle, and a lining of layered (stratified squamous) epithelium folded into ridges called rugae, which let it stretch.
layers.expert: Bacteria of the genus Lactobacillus dominate the healthy vagina; the lactic acid they make keeps its pH below 4.5, which protects against many other microbes.

title: Broad ligament
summary: A wide sheet of the abdominal lining draped over the uterus, tubes and ovaries.

layers.basics: The broad ligament is a fold of the thin membrane that lines the abdomen. It hangs over the uterus like a sheet over a line and reaches out to the walls of the pelvis.
layers.deeper: It is the uterus's main support. Its parts have their own names: the part that holds each tube is the mesosalpinx, the part that holds each ovary the mesovarium.
layers.expert: It is a fold of peritoneum. The ovarian blood and lymph vessels reach the ovary through the suspensory ligament, a part of the mesovarium; the uterine artery runs in its lower part.

title: Ligaments of the uterus and ovaries
summary: Bands of tissue that hold the uterus and the ovaries in place.

layers.basics: Several bands hold the uterus and ovaries where they are: some to the uterus, some to the walls of the pelvis.
layers.deeper: The ovarian ligament ties each ovary to the uterus; the suspensory ligament runs from the ovary to the pelvic wall and carries its vessels; the round ligament runs from near the tube forward to the labia majora; the uterosacral ligament ties the cervix to the back of the pelvis.
layers.expert: The cardinal ligaments, at the base of the broad ligament, carry the uterine arteries to the uterus. In this model these ligaments come from her sections and are shown together as one part.

facts: ovarian, suspensory, round, uterosacral and cardinal ligaments

title: Uterovesical pouch
summary: The shallow fold of the abdominal lining between the uterus and the bladder.

layers.basics: Where the lining of the abdomen passes from the bladder onto the front of the uterus it dips into a small pocket.
layers.deeper: Behind the uterus a deeper pocket, between the uterus and the rectum, is the lowest part of the abdominal cavity in a woman.
layers.expert: Fluid and infection in the abdomen tend to collect in the deeper pouch behind the uterus. The pouch in front, shown here from her sections, lies near the front of the vagina's top.

title: Endometrium
summary: The lining of the uterus, which thickens and is shed in each menstrual cycle.

layers.basics: The inside of the uterus is lined by a soft layer that grows thicker each month. If no pregnancy starts, most of it is shed: that is the menstrual period.
layers.deeper: It has two layers. The deeper stratum basalis stays; the stratum functionalis above it thickens under estrogen and progesterone and is the only layer shed.
layers.expert: Spiral arteries, branches of the uterine artery, supply the thickened functional layer. When progesterone falls at the end of a cycle they constrict and break, and the layer comes away. A cycle averages 28 days, usually from 21 to 32, and menstruation about five days.

title: Myometrium
summary: The thick wall of smooth muscle that makes up most of the uterus.

layers.basics: Most of the uterus is muscle: a thick wall that can stretch a great deal and squeeze hard.
layers.deeper: It is smooth muscle, outside the lining (endometrium) and inside a thin outer serous layer (perimetrium).
layers.expert: Its contractions push out the lining during a period and the baby during birth.

facts: the uterine wall: perimetrium, myometrium, endometrium

title: Uterine arteries and veins
summary: The blood vessels of the uterus, which grow much larger in pregnancy.

layers.basics: The uterus gets its blood mainly from the two uterine arteries, one on each side.
layers.deeper: Each uterine artery usually comes from a branch of the internal iliac artery in the pelvis, crosses in front of the ureter and reaches the side of the uterus near the cervix.
layers.expert: Its branches supply the uterus, the vagina, the tube and the ovary, where it commonly joins the ovarian artery. It enlarges a great deal in pregnancy. In this model the arteries and veins are from her sections, shown together.

title: Rectus femoris
summary: The front muscle of the thigh, one of the four of the quadriceps.

layers.basics: The rectus femoris runs down the front of the thigh to the kneecap. It helps you kick and lift your knee.
layers.deeper: It starts on the pelvis, at the anterior inferior iliac spine and just above the hip socket, so it crosses both the hip and the knee. With the other three muscles of the quadriceps it ends in the quadriceps tendon on the kneecap.
layers.expert: Below the kneecap the patellar ligament carries its pull on to the tibia. In this model it is the only muscle of her limbs that the atlas made from her sections.

facts: anterior inferior iliac spine and above the acetabulum

title: Eye muscles
summary: The six small muscles that turn each eye, and the one that lifts the upper lid.

layers.basics: Six muscles move each eye up, down and to the sides, and twist it a little. A seventh lifts the upper eyelid.
layers.deeper: Four straight muscles (the superior, inferior, medial and lateral rectus) start from a ring of tendon at the back of the eye socket; two oblique muscles, superior and inferior, approach the eye at an angle.
layers.expert: The lateral rectus turns the eye out, the medial rectus in; the superior and inferior rectus raise and lower it; the obliques add rotation. In this model they come from her sections, adjusted by the atlas makers.

title: Knee cartilage and menisci
summary: The smooth cartilage on the ends of the knee's bones, and the two C-shaped pads between them.

layers.basics: Between the thigh bone and the shin bone sit two C-shaped pads, the menisci, which fill the gap between the round end of the femur and the flatter top of the tibia.
layers.deeper: The menisci are fibrocartilage, thin at the inner edge and thick at the outer. They are attached to the tibia but not to the femur. The medial one moves less, because it is tied to the joint's capsule and to a ligament.
layers.expert: Parts of the menisci have no arterial blood supply and heal poorly. The medial meniscus is about 20 times more likely to be injured than the lateral one.

title: Knee ligaments
summary: The bands that hold the knee together: two crossing inside it and one on each side.

layers.basics: The knee is held by strong bands: two that cross inside the joint (the cruciate ligaments) and one on each side (the collateral ligaments).
layers.deeper: The anterior cruciate ligament resists over-straightening; the posterior, the stronger, stops the femur sliding forward off the tibia when the knee is bent and bearing weight. The collateral ligaments are tight when the leg is straight and resist sideways and twisting movement.
layers.expert: A hard blow to the outer side of a straight knee can injure, in turn, the medial collateral ligament, the medial meniscus and the anterior cruciate ligament. A torn cruciate ligament is often rebuilt with part of the patellar ligament.

title: Coccyx
summary: The tailbone: a few small vertebrae at the bottom of the spine.

layers.basics: The coccyx is the small tailbone at the very bottom of the spine, below the sacrum.
layers.deeper: It is made of three, four or five small vertebrae, which may be fused or separate. It joins the sacrum at a joint of fibrocartilage that allows a little movement.
layers.expert: Muscles of the pelvic floor attach to its front, and part of the gluteus maximus to its back.

title: Bronchopulmonary segments
summary: The divisions of each lobe of a lung, each with its own airway and its own artery.

layers.basics: Each lobe of a lung is divided into segments. A segment gets air from its own branch of the airway and blood from its own artery.
layers.deeper: The right lung has three lobes and the left two; every lobe holds several segments. Each is fed by its own tertiary bronchus.
layers.expert: Because a segment has its own airway and blood supply, a surgeon can remove one diseased segment and leave the rest of the lobe working. In this model her lungs are made of these segments, traced from her sections.

facts: its own tertiary bronchus and artery

title: Cardiac veins
summary: The veins of the heart's own muscle, which gather into the coronary sinus.

layers.basics: The heart's muscle needs blood like any other, and its used blood comes back through the cardiac veins.
layers.deeper: The great, middle and small cardiac veins run beside the coronary arteries and empty into the coronary sinus, a large thin-walled vein in the groove at the back of the heart between the atria and the ventricles.
layers.expert: The coronary sinus empties into the right atrium, just above the opening of the inferior vena cava. The anterior cardiac veins bypass it and open straight into the right atrium.

facts: the coronary sinus, then the right atrium

title: Bile ducts
summary: The branching ducts that carry bile from the liver to the gallbladder and the small intestine.

layers.basics: The liver makes about a litre of bile a day. It drains through a tree of ducts into the small intestine, and between meals some is stored in the gallbladder.
layers.deeper: The right and left hepatic ducts join as the common hepatic duct; the cystic duct, 1 to 2 cm long, joins it from the gallbladder to make the common bile duct, which meets the pancreatic duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla in the wall of the duodenum.
layers.expert: A ring of smooth muscle at the ampulla controls the flow of bile and pancreatic juice. The gallbladder, 8 to 10 cm long, can concentrate bile up to tenfold. In this model the ducts of the liver and the pancreas are shown together.

title: Liver segments
summary: The eight parts of the liver that each have their own blood supply and bile drainage.

layers.basics: Surgeons divide the liver into eight segments. Each has its own blood coming in and its own bile going out, so one can be removed without harming the others.
layers.deeper: The scheme is named after the French surgeon Claude Couinaud. A branch of the portal vein, the hepatic artery and the bile duct runs through the middle of each segment; hepatic veins drain blood from its edges.
layers.expert: Segment I is the caudate lobe at the back; II and III lie left of the falciform ligament and IV right of it; V to VIII make up the right lobe. A surgeon cuts along the hepatic veins at the segments' edges. In this model her liver is made of these segments, traced from her sections.

facts: portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct branch

title: Greater omentum
summary: An apron of fatty membrane that hangs from the stomach in front of the intestines.

layers.basics: The greater omentum hangs down like an apron from the stomach over the intestines. It is mostly fat.
layers.deeper: It is a double sheet of the abdominal lining folded back on itself, so four layers thick, with many blood vessels and patches of immune cells (milky spots, which hold macrophages).
layers.expert: It stores fat, helps defend against infection and can wrap round an inflamed or injured spot in the abdomen, which may limit the spread of infection. In 1906 the surgeon Rutherford Morison called it the "abdominal policeman". In her model it hangs from where her stomach would be: the atlas has no stomach.

title: Mouth: gums, palate and lining
summary: The soft tissues of the mouth: the gums round the teeth, the roof of the mouth and the lining of the cheeks.

layers.basics: The roof of the mouth has a bony front part (the hard palate) and a soft muscular back part (the soft palate). The gums cover the jaw bones round the teeth.
layers.deeper: The hard palate is formed by the maxillary and palatine bones; the soft palate is mostly skeletal muscle, with the uvula hanging from its back edge. The inside of the cheeks is lined by layered epithelium that is not keratinized.
layers.expert: In her model these tissues come from her sections, modelled with the guidance of atlases of the mouth.

title: Salivary glands
summary: Three pairs of glands that make most of the saliva.

layers.basics: Saliva comes mostly from three pairs of glands: in front of the ears, under the jaw and under the tongue. An adult makes 1 to 1.5 litres a day.
layers.deeper: The parotid glands lie between the skin and the chewing muscle near the ears, and their ducts open near the second upper molar; the submandibular glands lie in the floor of the mouth; the sublingual glands below the tongue. Small glands in the cheeks, lips, palate and tongue add more.
layers.expert: Saliva is about 99.4 % water. Its amylase starts breaking down starch, lysozyme kills bacteria, and mucus makes food slippery to swallow.
